subtype: Recognizing Warning Signs & Seeking Professional Help
passage: Selin had been working at a café in Istanbul while finishing university. For months she slept badly, skipped meals and said "fine" when anyone asked. She stopped going to her Friday dance class. Her friend Rafael noticed she hadn't laughed in weeks. One evening he found her sitting in the storeroom, staring at the shelves. "I don't feel anything," she said. "I'm tired all the time and nothing seems worth it." Rafael sat with her. "That sounds heavy. Would you talk to someone? The university has a counsellor." She shrugged, but he helped her book an appointment on his phone right there. The next week she went. She said afterwards it was strange but a relief to say it all out loud.

qa.q: What class did Selin stop going to?
qa.a: She stopped going to her Friday dance class.

qa.q: What does Selin's "I don't feel anything" suggest about her state?
qa.a: It suggests she was deeply exhausted and emotionally numb, and had lost hope, which are warning signs to take seriously.

qa.q: What made Rafael's response helpful?
qa.a: He listened without judging and helped her book a counsellor appointment immediately, turning concern into a concrete step.

qa.q: How might Rafael feel after Selin went to the counsellor?
qa.a: He might feel relieved and hopeful, but also keep checking on her since recovery takes time. 🤍

grounding: It shows a young woman's prolonged exhaustion and hopelessness noticed by a friend who helps her get professional help early.

subtype: Recognizing Warning Signs & Seeking Professional Help
passage: In the engineering college library, Anand noticed his lab partner Lalremsiami had changed. She used to be the first to answer; now she stared at her screen for an hour without typing. She was always tired, even after weekends. She stopped eating in the mess with the group. One afternoon he asked quietly, "Are you okay?" She laughed, a thin laugh. "Just burned out. I'll push through." But then she said, "Some mornings I can't get out of bed." Anand remembered a poster about the campus wellness centre. He said, "I'll walk with you there, if you want." She hesitated for two days, then texted him: "Okay." After her first session, she told him the counsellor suggested also seeing a doctor. She was going next week.

qa.q: Where did Anand offer to walk with Lalremsiami?
qa.a: He offered to walk with her to the campus wellness centre.

qa.q: What does Lalremsiami's thin laugh suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she felt low and worn out but was trying to brush it off, hiding how much she was struggling.

qa.q: What did Anand do well in this situation?
qa.a: He noticed the changes, asked gently, and offered practical support by walking with her to get professional help.

qa.q: How might Lalremsiami feel about Anand's offer?
qa.a: She may have felt embarrassed at first, which is why she hesitated, but also relieved that someone noticed and cared.

grounding: It shows a friend noticing a young woman's burnout warning signs and helping her seek professional help.

subtype: Recognizing Warning Signs & Seeking Professional Help
passage:
Kamal,
You asked why I've been so quiet on our calls. I'll try to be honest.
For about two months I've felt flat. I sleep ten hours and wake up tired. I've stopped going to the gym. I skip messages, even yours. Last week I sat in front of my assignment for three hours and wrote one line. I kept telling myself it's just a phase.
But I read your message about your cousin, how she waited too long to get help. That scared me.
So I booked an appointment at the student counselling centre for Thursday. I'm nervous. I don't know what to say.
Can you call me Thursday evening, after? Just to talk.
Kiran

qa.q: When is Kiran's appointment at the student counselling centre?
qa.a: It is on Thursday.

qa.q: What made Kiran decide to book an appointment?
qa.a: Reading about Kamal's cousin who waited too long scared Kiran into seeing that the flatness was more than a phase.

qa.q: What is wise about how Kiran is handling this?
qa.a: Kiran is naming the warning signs honestly, getting professional help early and asking a friend for support afterwards.

qa.q: How might Kamal feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Kamal might feel worried but also relieved and trusted, glad Kiran is getting help and wants Kamal involved.

grounding: A young adult's letter shows recognising prolonged exhaustion and withdrawal and seeking professional help early.

subtype: Recognizing Warning Signs & Seeking Professional Help
passage: So, Vaibhav, you asked how I knew it wasn't just a bad week. Honestly, I didn't, not at first. Third year, I was sleeping ten hours and still waking up tired. I stopped going to badminton, which I love. My roommate would ask about dinner and I'd say 'later' till the mess closed. The scary bit was this flat feeling, like nothing I did would matter anyway. It went on and on. What finally moved me was my younger cousin on a video call asking, 'Yamini didi, why don't you laugh anymore?' The next day I booked a slot with the campus counsellor. My hands were shaking in the waiting room. She didn't fix everything in one session, but she took it seriously, and we made a plan that included seeing a doctor too. I wish I'd gone earlier.

qa.q: Which sport did Yamini stop going to?
qa.a: Badminton, which she loves.

qa.q: Why did the flat feeling scare Yamini?
qa.a: It felt like nothing she did would matter anyway; that hopelessness scared her more than the tiredness because it was so unlike her.

qa.q: What does Yamini's story suggest about when to seek help?
qa.a: When exhaustion, withdrawal or hopelessness keep going and do not lift, reaching a counsellor or doctor early helps; she wishes she had not waited 🙏

qa.q: What might it have been like for her cousin to notice she didn't laugh anymore?
qa.a: The cousin probably missed the old Yamini and felt puzzled or worried, and that simple question made the change visible to Yamini herself.

grounding: A student tells a friend how she noticed lasting exhaustion, withdrawal and hopelessness and sought professional help.

subtype: Recognizing Warning Signs & Seeking Professional Help
passage: I'm Mohit, Divyansh's roommate since first year. Something shifted around October. He stopped coming to the canteen with us, left assignments half done, and his lamp stayed off even when he was clearly awake. When I joked that he was becoming a monk, he didn't even smile. I wasn't sure what was going on, maybe exams, maybe home. I didn't want to be dramatic. But after a few weeks I sat on the edge of his bed and said, 'You seem really low, and I'm worried. Not judging.' He shrugged and said he was just tired all the time and didn't see the point of much. I told him about the student wellness centre and offered to walk there with him. He said no. Two days later he asked, 'Does that offer still stand?' It did.

qa.q: When did Mohit notice something shift in Divyansh?
qa.a: Around October.

qa.q: Why did Mohit hesitate before saying anything?
qa.a: Mohit was not sure what was going on and worried about seeming dramatic or intrusive.

qa.q: Which part of Mohit's approach helped, and why?
qa.a: He named his worry without judging and made help concrete by offering to walk to the wellness centre with him, then left the door open after a no.

qa.q: How might things have gone if Mohit had kept joking instead of asking?
qa.a: Divyansh might have stayed hidden behind being 'just tired', and the warning signs could have gone unaddressed for much longer.

grounding: A roommate notices signs of withdrawal and hopelessness and gently helps a friend toward professional support.
